name: Brow microshading / powder brows
lead: Brow microshading, also sold as powder brows or ombre brows, is a form of cosmetic eyebrow tattooing that gives a soft, filled-in, makeup-like finish rather than individual hair-like strokes. People choose it to make sparse, patchy or short brows look fuller and more defined without drawing them in each day, and it sits within the wider field of permanent makeup, in which pigment is placed in the dermis.[1][2]

It is usually discussed next to microblading, which uses a handheld tool to draw hair-like strokes. Wikipedia's microblading article does not describe microshading or powder brows by name, so details of the shaded technique rest on practitioner descriptions of a stippled or gradient fill.[2]
Reference works report that cosmetic brow tattoos fade over time, are hard to remove completely, and carry risks including allergic reactions, infection, granulomas and pigment migration.[1][2]

chain: Pigment is tattooed into the upper dermis in a stippled or gradient pattern
Brow area looks filled with a soft powdered finish
Fuller, more defined brows without daily makeup
angle.text: Microshading fills gaps and shapes the brow with a soft shaded look, so the eyes appear more framed. It is also used where brow hair has been lost through aging, illness, chemotherapy or genetic conditions.

infobox: About 12 to 18 months, per a review of microblading[3]
No federal technician standard; FDA treats inks as cosmetics[1]

paras: Permanent makeup uses tattooing to place pigment in the dermis, and is used for eyeliner, lip color and eyebrows, including for people who have lost brow hair through aging, illness, chemotherapy or genetic conditions.[1] Microblading deposits pigment into the upper dermis with a manual blade of stacked needles; a 2021 review in the Indian Dermatology Online Journal describes it as superficial micropigmentation reaching the papillary dermis and notes its use for alopecia totalis, hypothyroidism and chemotherapy-induced madarosis.[3] Microshading and powder brows are marketed as producing a shaded fill instead of strokes.[2]

Brow tattoos fade with sun exposure, skin type, products and medications. Microblading-type treatments are reported to last up to about two years, with touch-ups often recommended after about six weeks and then every 12 to 18 months.[2] The 2021 review puts semi-permanent results at about 12 to 18 months.[3] Permanent makeup removal can be difficult or sometimes impossible; options include laser, dermabrasion, surgical excision and chemical removal.[1]

Common short-term effects include itching, redness and swelling. Less common complications include allergic reactions, infection, granulomas, keloids and, rarely, swelling or burning during MRI scans linked to some pigments.[1] Wikipedia lists misapplied pigment, migration, color change and hyperpigmentation as common problems of microblading, and bloodborne infections if sterility is not maintained.[2] The 2021 review says rising popularity has brought more untrained practitioners and more side effects.[3]

In the United States the FDA reviews inks as cosmetics, some pigments are not approved for skin use, and technician requirements vary by state.[1] In Canada microblading is regulated as a personal service by individual provinces.[2]

No studies found on microshading or powder brows themselves. Published work on the neighboring technique includes a 2021 review of microblading,[3] and case reports of granulomatous reactions after brow pigment procedures are listed in Wikipedia's microblading references.[2]

timeline.event: British tattoo artist Sutherland MacDonald is the earliest well-documented permanent-makeup practitioner, working in London.[1]
Cosmetic eyebrow tattooing becomes more common in the US and Asia.[2]
Microblading, then called eyebrow embroidery, becomes popular in Singapore.[2]
Microblading becomes popular in the US and Canada.[2]

card.summary: Tattooed, soft-shaded brow fill that fades over time; closely related to microblading, with little published research of its own.
card.note: A tattoo: pigment reactions, infection and difficult removal are documented.

quick.overview:
Microshading or powder brows is a cosmetic tattoo that fills the brows with a soft, makeup-like gradient instead of drawn hairs. It is offered at tattoo and beauty studios.

The sources reviewed describe brow tattooing generally rather than this technique specifically, so published evidence on it by name is thin.
quick.mechanism: A technician deposits pigment, commonly iron-oxide based, into the skin to create a shaded brow shape. Results fade gradually and touch-ups are typically recommended.
quick.risks: Reported risks include allergic reactions, infection, granulomas, keloids and pigment migration, and removal can be hard. Regulation varies; in the US there is no federal technician standard.
